name: Celtic lime-washing hair bleach

lead: Around the first century BC the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus wrote that the Gauls kept their hair naturally blond and enhanced it by constantly washing it in lime-water. He added that they combed it back from the forehead to the nape, giving a shaggy, horse-mane look.

The appearance payoff described is lighter, brighter hair and a bold, voluminous swept-back style. The account is a secondhand classical description; no modern study has tested the method, and chemists would expect lime to lighten and stiffen hair through its alkalinity.

paras: As Diodorus describes it, the wash was repeated regularly and the hair was then combed back so it stood thick and coarse. Details of the preparation are not given in the source, and this wiki does not provide a modern recipe.

Lime-water is strongly alkaline. Alkaline products are known to roughen hair and irritate skin and eyes, and Diodorus himself says the treatment left hair heavy and coarse. The historical account is not guidance for modern use.

chain: Alkaline wash lightens colour and stiffens strands
angle.text: Classical sources say Gaulish men used lime-water to push naturally blond hair lighter and to give it a thick, swept-back shape. It is documented as a historical practice rather than a tested hair treatment.

lead: Celtic lime-washing is the practice, described by the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, of Gauls washing their hair in lime-water to lighten it and to style it back from the face [1].

According to Diodorus (Book V, chapter 28), the Gauls were naturally blond but used artificial means to heighten the colour, constantly washing their hair in lime-water and combing it from the forehead back over the crown to the nape [1]. He says the result made them look like Satyrs and Pans, and that the hair became so heavy and coarse that it resembled horses' manes [1].

For people interested in hair appearance, it is cited as an early example of deliberate hair lightening and of using a mineral wash to hold a dramatic style. Diodorus compiled his history largely from earlier writers and probably did not visit Gaul himself, so the account is secondhand. No archaeological or scientific study of the method is cited here.

paras: Diodorus says the Gauls were tall with light skin and blond hair, and that they enhanced the blond by artificial means [1]. He describes them as constantly washing their hair with lime-water and drawing it back, so that it looked like the hair of Satyrs and Pans and became thick like a horse's mane [1].
Translations vary in detail, and Diodorus's own sources, such as Posidonius, were earlier writers, so how widespread the practice was is not established.
Lime-water is alkaline, and alkaline treatments are generally associated with rough, dry hair and skin or eye irritation. Diodorus himself notes the coarse, heavy texture the treatment produced [1].
